change_since_last_report:
The previous compatible dossier is dated 18 June 2026, when NZD/USD was 0.5833. Spot is now 0.58877, 0.9% higher. The thesis has bifurcated: it was flat at both horizons and is now clearly directional in opposite directions.

**Stance and score changes.** Tactically the net stance moved from **Neutral (conviction 2, confidence 57, weighted score −0.0314) to Bullish (conviction 3, confidence 55, weighted score +0.3514)** — a swing of +0.3828 in the weighted score, the largest single-cycle move in this currency's recent history and driven overwhelmingly by the 8 July policy inflection. Strategically the net stance moved from **Neutral (conviction 2, confidence 55, weighted score 0.0000) to Bearish (conviction 2, confidence 53, weighted score −0.1258)**. The G10+SGD ranking moved from 6/11 at both horizons to 3/11 tactically and 8/11 strategically.

**Factors that changed stance.** Seven of ten moved. Factor 1 (Policy & Rates) moved from Neutral/Neutral to **Bullish/Neutral** because the RBNZ delivered the first hike in more than three years on 8 July and told the market more are likely. Factor 2 (Inflation & Growth) moved from Neutral/Neutral to **Bullish/Neutral** on a 4.1% CPI that beat the Bank's own expected peak, a PMI at a five-year high of 59.7 and business confidence at 56.1. Factor 3 (Risk Appetite) moved from Bullish/Neutral to **Neutral/Bearish** as the Strait of Hormuz situation re-escalated and Brent round-tripped from roughly $70 to $90. Factor 4 (Flows & Positioning) moved from Neutral/Neutral to **Bullish/Neutral** as the CFTC non-commercial short widened from −25,285 on 30 June to −30,027 on 28 July, adding into a rising currency. Factor 6 (Guidance) moved from Bullish/Neutral to **Bullish/Bullish** on the explicit "further OCR increases appear likely" language and the Committee's statement that a lower exchange rate could add to inflation pressures. Factor 7 (Event Risk) moved from Neutral/Neutral to **Neutral/Bearish** because the 7 November general election has entered the strategic horizon. Factor 8 (Fiscal) moved from Neutral/Neutral to **Neutral/Bearish** for the same reason, coupled to Fitch's published negative trigger. Factor 9 (Market Structure) moved from Bearish/Neutral to **Neutral/Neutral** because spot has reclaimed all four moving averages. Factor 10 (USD Liquidity) moved from Bearish/Neutral to **Bullish/Neutral** as the broad dollar index fell and the Fed balance sheet expanded. Factor 5 (External Balance) is the only factor to hold its tactical stance, moving from Bearish/Neutral to **Bearish/Bearish** as Fonterra cut the 2026/27 farmgate forecast and oil rose.

**Signposts that triggered.** Five of seven. The OCR signpost, which was set at "OCR 2.25% held 27 May, track peak ~3.0–3.28%", **triggered on the hawkish side** — the Bank hiked. The GDT signpost, at "−2.8% on 16 June, whole milk powder $3,589 per tonne", **triggered on the bearish side** — the index is lower on balance and whole milk powder is $103 a tonne cheaper at $3,486. The moving-average signpost, which recorded spot below the 50-day, 100-day and 200-day, **triggered on the bullish side** — spot has reclaimed all of them. The CFTC signpost, at "−31.6k net short and widening", **did not trigger** — the non-commercial net has run −25,285 to −31,086 to −30,027 through July, so the short is essentially unchanged from mid-June and is still widening on trend rather than covering. The broad dollar signpost, at 119.5, moved to 120.71, which is a **mildly adverse** outcome contrary to the prior dossier's expectation of dollar softening. The VIX at 16.4 is now 17.09 and the NZ–US ten-year spread at +8 basis points is now +6, both essentially unchanged.

**New catalysts since 18 June.** The 2 September Monetary Policy Statement with its first published OCR track since May; the 7 November general election, now inside the strategic horizon; the collapse of the 17 June Hormuz memorandum of understanding and the subsequent tanker attacks; Fonterra's 13 July farmgate downgrade; and China's second-quarter GDP miss at 4.3%.

**Summary.** The thesis is **strengthening tactically and weakening strategically** since 18 June, because the RBNZ has converted a possible hiking cycle into an actual one — which is worth a great deal over four weeks and, on the arithmetic that a 3.25% terminal still leaves New Zealand yielding less than the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Norway, considerably less over six months.
seasonality: One documented seasonal pattern is relevant inside both horizons. The New Zealand dairy season runs from 1 June, and national milk production ramps from a winter trough through August and September toward its October peak; GlobalDairyTrade volumes rise accordingly through the spring flush. That supply seasonality is a mechanical headwind for auction prices through the tactical window and the first half of the strategic window, and it compounds the demand-side weakness already visible in Chinese activity. The second relevant pattern is the New Zealand electoral cycle: with an election on 7 November, the September to November period will carry an unusual density of fiscal announcements and pre-election spending commitments, which historically produces wider swap spreads and thinner liquidity in the front end of the New Zealand curve. No other seasonal pattern is asserted; the frequently cited "Q3 antipodean weakness" effect is not supported by a documented source in this research and is therefore excluded.
assumptions: Canonical spot and cross-rate set. All spot rates, crosses, performance calculations, moving averages and realised volatilities are computed from a single daily-close dataset with a final observation of 31 July 2026, so that every cross is arithmetically consistent (NZD/JPY = NZD/USD x USD/JPY, and so on). NZD/USD is taken as 0.58877. Note that the RBNZ's own B1 table records NZD/USD at 0.58660 on 31 July 2026, a difference of approximately 22 pips reflecting different closing conventions and time stamps. Commercial quotes for the same date run as low as approximately 0.5873, and at least one vendor describes the July gain as over 3% against the 2.29% computed here. All targets, levels and pip calculations are stated relative to 0.58877 and should be adjusted proportionally if a different convention is used; the basis uncertainty is roughly 0.4%.

Implied volatility and risk reversals are unobtainable and are stated as gaps, not estimated. No free or public venue publishes NZD/USD OTC 1-month or 3-month at-the-money implied volatility, an implied-volatility percentile, or a 25-delta risk reversal for mid-2026. A dedicated search across retail and institutional venues returned nothing citable. Rather than substitute a proxy, this dossier reports realised volatility only (20-day 7.52%, 60-day 7.24%, 90-day 7.69%, computed from the canonical close series) and sets Factor 9's confidence at 48 tactical and 46 strategic accordingly. No risk-reversal figure appears anywhere in this dossier and no variance risk premium is asserted.

The valuation table is a REER-relative method, not an OECD PPP table. The framework calls for a PPP deviation table. OECD PPP-based exchange-rate deviations were not retrievable for this cycle, so the table is constructed from BIS real broad effective exchange rates: each currency's June 2026 REER is expressed as a deviation from its own mean over the available 30-month window, and the bilateral figure is the New Zealand deviation minus the peer deviation. This is the same method used across the other dossiers in this cycle, so the table is internally consistent with them.

Forward points are CIP-derived, not traded quotes. Traded NZD/USD forward points were not sourceable from a free public venue. The forwards in the Forward vs Spot Decomposition are derived by covered interest parity from an approximate 90 basis point short-rate differential - a New Zealand three-month rate near 2.75%, interpolated between the 2.50% cash rate and the 3.45% one-year swap, against a US three-month rate near 3.65% anchored on SOFR at 3.65%. The implied appreciation of 0.90% annualised should be treated as an approximation with an uncertainty of roughly plus or minus 15 basis points.

Cross-currency basis is largely unobservable. The 3-month EUR/USD cross-currency basis runs approximately flat. The 3-month JPY/USD and 3-month NZD/USD basis levels could not be obtained from any free public source and are stated as gaps rather than estimated. Factor 10's confidence reflects this.

Positioning data are vendor-sourced and internally inconsistent, and the primary series was changed after verification. New Zealand dollar Commitments of Traders data are not in this cycle's cached COT extract and were sourced from vendor renderings of the CFTC release. The CFTC non-commercial category is used as primary because it is the only series with a continuous reproducible history: -25,285 (30 June), -27,201 (7 July), -29,002 (14 July), -31,086 (21 July), -30,027 (28 July), with open interest of 105,128. A separate vendor speculative-net series reports -62.8k, -50.0k and -47.7k through July, implying substantial covering; it cannot be reconciled with the non-commercial history and is not used as primary. An earlier draft relied on that vendor series and described the position as covering; the correction reverses the direction of the four-week change and Factor 4's confidence is now 52 tactical and 50 strategic.

Carry and carry-to-vol convention. Carry is stated as the annualised policy-rate differential (New Zealand minus peer). Carry-to-volatility ratios divide that differential, in percent, by the trailing 60-day realised volatility of the relevant cross, in percent, because 3-month implied volatility is unobservable for these crosses. Ratios computed against implied volatility would differ where implied exceeds realised. For Singapore, where MAS operates a NEER band rather than a policy rate, SORA at approximately 0.97% is used as the rate proxy and no carry-to-vol ratio is computed.

Middle East crisis framing. The Strait of Hormuz disruption is treated throughout as a five-month-old crisis that re-escalated in July 2026, not as a new July event. It began in late February 2026; a memorandum of understanding on 17 June produced the oil price collapse the RBNZ cited on 8 July; that memorandum collapsed and the blockade was reimposed in mid-July; Iranian forces attacked two escorted tankers in the final days of July. This matters because the RBNZ's 8 July decision was explicitly conditioned on current oil futures pricing being significantly lower than assumed in the May Statement, an assumption Brent invalidated within days of the decision.

Peer macro figures are compiled from national sources at differing reference dates. The macro comparison table draws on the cycle's shared OECD and BIS reference snapshot plus national statistical agencies and central banks. Reference periods differ by country. New Zealand GDP is reported as 1.47% year-on-year on the OECD through-the-year basis for cross-country comparability; Statistics New Zealand's own annual-average measure for the same quarter is 0.8%, and the quarterly figure of 0.8% is common to both.

Conflicting risk-metric vintages. The VIX is taken as 17.09 at the 30 July close from the cached Cboe series. At least one secondary source reports a VIX of 20.66 on 29 July. The discrepancy is flagged rather than resolved, and Factor 3's confidence reflects it. Similarly, the US high-yield option-adjusted spread is reported at 284 basis points on 30 July from one vendor and as 2.87% by another for the same period; the two are consistent to within three basis points.

Verification pass and confidence reductions. Every headline figure was spot-checked against its cited URL after drafting by an independent verification agent, and the result was applied rather than set aside. Nine of the ten factors had confidence reduced. The material findings were: the positioning series was wrong-signed (see the positioning assumption above); a BNZ quotation used four times could not be found in the cited article and has been replaced with the passage the article actually carries, that historically low New Zealand interest rates remain an enduring headwind to any NZD recovery; BNZ's published technical levels are initial support 0.5625-0.5630 and resistance 0.5850, not the 0.5750 support originally attributed; the VIX printed 20.66 on 29 July before the 17.09 close on 30 July, so the tactical risk read has been re-characterised as a spike that retraced; the labour-market consensus is 5.4% (RBNZ, Westpac) to 5.5% (ANZ, ASB) with bank forecasts of a June-quarter GDP contraction of 0.1-0.3%; China's Q2 GDP miss was a quarterly event, with first-half growth of 4.7% inside the official 4.5-5% range; an ANZ NZD/USD forecast of 0.67 for end-2027 could not be substantiated and has been removed; and the estimate that China takes roughly 40% of New Zealand's dairy exports is best available, flagged.

Several sources are rolling data pages rather than dated snapshots. Citations 3, 4, 5, 17, 19, 22, 31, 32, 33 and 40 resolve but publish live data, so the specific figures attributed to them - the RBNZ Trade Weighted Index at 66.87, the New Zealand and Australian sovereign yields, the two-year swap at 3.81%, the 2.53% two-year inflation expectation, the NZX 50 at 13,699.28, the ANZ commodity index changes and the BIS real effective exchange rates underpinning the entire valuation table - cannot be reproduced from the URL at a later date. They are best available, flagged, and the confidences of Factors 1, 2, 5, 9 and 10 have been reduced accordingly. All moving averages, realised volatilities, cross rates and range figures are computed from the canonical 400-observation close series and are similarly unverifiable externally.
